requirement_title: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.
requirement_text:
# REQ-2297: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2297
Type: feature

## Requirement

MessagePack generated code is not decorated with the `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage` attribute. Because it is very hard to write good coverage for generated MessagePack code, it may skew coverage numbers, especially on large projects with a lot of generated code.

Solution requested: "I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.  I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too."

Alternatives considered by the author: none; "it is close to impossible to write good coverage for generated code as it covers many edge cases."

## Acceptance criteria

- All generated code is decorated with `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage`.
- No new setting or option is required to get the attribute. ("I do not feel like a setting is needed")
- An opt-out setting would be acceptable but is optional. ("setting would be fine to have too")
- The generated code still compiles on every supported target framework (the attribute must exist there or be conditionally emitted). (derived)
- Existing verified generator snapshots are updated to include the attribute. (derived)

## Notes from discussion

- b-kurczynski-dl suggests a coverage-tool workaround instead: exclude `obj\\.*\.g\.cs$` in the `dotnet-coverage` settings XML.
- armadavalor offers a PR: add `[global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` (and possibly `GeneratedCode`) to the types emitted by the templates under `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/` (formatters, string-key formatters, enum/union formatters, resolvers), update the verified snapshots, no setting. Asks AArnott whether he would accept it or prefer to point users at coverage-tool configuration. No maintainer reply in the thread.
- Ambiguity driver: scope (all generated types vs formatters only) and setting (unconditional vs opt-out) are both open.

findings.claim: Every new attribute is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. As a result, generated code compiled for netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework gets no `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage` at all. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` exists on both (.NET Framework 4.0+ and .NET Standard 2.0) and can be applied to classes, so the exclusion is not needed for compilation. It breaks the 'All generated code is decorated' criterion for a very common class of consumers (netstandard2.0 libraries, net472 apps). The README states the wrong availability claim as fact.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageDownlevelTargetsTests.GeneratedTypes_AreExcludedFromCodeCoverage_OnDownlevelTargets with InlineData NETSTANDARD2_0 and NETFRAMEWORK. On head the generated formatter and resolver symbols carry no ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute, although the attribute type resolves.

findings.claim: Every new attribute is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` already exists in .NET Framework 4.0+ and netstandard2.0, and it is valid on classes there. So a consumer project targeting net472/net48 or netstandard2.0 gets no attribute on any generated formatter or resolver. The guard is not needed for compilation, so the requirement 'all generated code is decorated' is not met on those targets. Multi-targeted libraries will also report different coverage per target framework.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageLegacyTfmTests.GeneratedTypesCarryAttribute_WhenTargetSymbolDefined("NETSTANDARD2_0") and ("NETFRAMEWORK"). Each drives MessagePackGenerator with that preprocessor symbol defined, then asserts that the generated resolver and formatter symbols carry ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute. On head, the #if makes the attribute inactive and the assertion fails.

findings.claim: no test in the suite detects swap-boolean at src/MessagePack/GeneratedMessagePackResolverAttribute.cs:34

receipt_plan.detail: public bool ExcludeFromCodeCoverage { get; set; } = true; -> public bool ExcludeFromCodeCoverage { get; set; } = false;

findings.claim: the change's own tests do not catch mutants at src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/AnalyzerOptions.cs:206; the existing suite does

receipt_plan.detail: AnalyzerOptions.cs:206 swap-boolean: public bool ExcludeFromCodeCoverage { get; init; } = true; -> public bool ExcludeFromCodeCoverage { get; init; } = false;

hunches.claim: The #if guard `!NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` omits the attribute on netstandard2.0/.NET Framework builds, which contradicts the requirement that ALL generated code carry ExcludeFromCodeCoverage. ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute has existed since .NET Framework 4.0 and netstandard2.0, so the guard looks unnecessary. Users targeting those frameworks, including Unity-style consumers, still get coverage skew.

receipt_plan.detail: Regenerate the snapshot for a netstandard2.0 or net472 compilation. Check that the generated formatter contains no ExcludeFromCodeCoverage once the preprocessor symbols are defined. Compile a sample with a target that defines NETSTANDARD2_0 and confirm the attribute is absent.

hunches.claim: CompositeResolverTemplate emits the attribute unconditionally, bypassing the new Options.Generator.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage opt-out used in every other template. A user who sets ExcludeFromCodeCoverage=false still gets the attribute on composite resolvers, and the generated output is inconsistent.

receipt_plan.detail: Generate a composite resolver with [GeneratedMessagePackResolver(ExcludeFromCodeCoverage=false)] semantics and assert the output does not contain ExcludeFromCodeCoverage. It currently does.

hunches.claim: The change to the nesting emitter, `{` to `{\r\n`, alters the whitespace of generated output for nested types with constraints. This may break users' checked-in or snapshot generator output and is unrelated to the requirement. It is a compatibility-visible output change.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun the snapshot tests for nested generic types with constraints. Diff the output against base for changes unrelated to the attribute.

hunches.claim: The opt-out is read only from the [GeneratedMessagePackResolver] attribute. Formatters generated without a resolver attribute, such as the default resolver or assemblies with no attribute, fall back to the default of true and cannot be opted out. The opt-out is therefore not available everywhere generated code is emitted.

receipt_plan.detail: Generate formatters with no [GeneratedMessagePackResolver] attribute or with a different resolver config. Assert that no opt-out path exists and that the attribute is always emitted.

hunches.claim: The CompositeResolver template emits the attribute unconditionally and ignores Options.Generator.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage. The other templates honor the opt-out, so with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage=false the composite resolver is still decorated. The README states that opting out removes the attribute, and the opt-out test asserts it is absent from every generated file, so the test may not exercise a composite resolver.

receipt_plan.detail: Set ExcludeFromCodeCoverage=false and generate a CompositeResolver (the tests do not cover one). Assert that the output does not contain the attribute.

hunches.claim: Only top-level generated types and the nested FormatterCache helper types are decorated. Nesting partial types emitted by EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces are user-declared partials and are left undecorated, which may be fine. The TransformUtilities change from '{' to '{\r\n' alters generated output for all nested generic-constrained types and is not related to this requirement.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun the snapshot tests and inspect the diffs for nested types with constraints. Check that only the intended whitespace change appears.

hunches.claim: The composite resolver template emits ExcludeFromCodeCoverage unconditionally and ignores the new ExcludeFromCodeCoverage option. The opt-out test never exercises CompositeResolverTemplate, since TestSource has no [CompositeResolver] and the test's >=5-file count is met by other outputs. Any mutation to the composite template's attribute emission (removal, or wrapping in the option check) survives.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/CompositeResolverTemplate.cs:27 delete-statement: remove the '#if...ExcludeFromCodeCoverage...#endif' text from the Write call; expected to survive because no test source uses a composite resolver generator input, so CodeCoverageExclusionTests never sees that file.

hunches.claim: The opt-out test sets ExcludeFromCodeCoverage=false only via the [GeneratedMessagePackResolver] attribute. The parse in AnalyzerUtilities (`is not false`) is never tested for an explicit true value or for a missing argument. Mutating the default or the `is not false` comparison could pass if both flipped paths are not asserted. Also, the TestSource.Replace silently becomes a no-op if the attribute text changes, and then the Assert.False would fail loudly. The real gap is that no test covers a type-level/default flow separately from the attribute default (`= true` in GeneratedMessagePackResolverAttribute).

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Utils/AnalyzerUtilities.cs:76 swap-boolean: `is not false` -> `is true`; expected to survive in the default test only if GetSingleNamedArgumentValue returns the attribute default, but AllGeneratedTypesAreExcludedFromCodeCoverage omits the named arg so it would fail. Run to confirm; the remaining risk is the attribute default `= true` mutated to false, which is masked.

hunches.claim: The guard test checks only the textual `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` wrapper; no test compiles generated code against netstandard2.0 or net472 to prove the guard is correct. The guard macro names are not verified to be defined, and the guard also hides the attribute on netstandard2.1, which does have it. Mutating the guard text consistently in templates and tests would pass.

receipt_plan.detail: All templates' guard string `!NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` -> `!NETSTANDARD2_0` or `true`; the test's Guard constant would also need changing, so a coherent mutant survives. No compile-against-framework test exists.

hunches.claim: The TransformUtilities change (`{` -> `{\r\n` when type constraints exist) alters output for nesting types with constraints, but no test in the diff targets it. Only the withheld snapshots could catch it, and only if a snapshot has a constrained nesting generic type.

receipt_plan.detail: TransformUtilities.cs:58 swap: `"{\r\n"` -> `"{"` for the anyConstraints branch; expected to survive unless an existing snapshot test has a nested generic type with constraints. Rerun the snapshot tests to check.

hunches.claim: CompositeResolverTemplate emits the attribute unconditionally and ignores the new opt-out. The README says the opt-out `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver(ExcludeFromCodeCoverage = false)]` applies to 'all generated formatters and resolvers', but a generated composite resolver stays decorated with no way to opt out.

receipt_plan.detail: CompositeResolverTemplate.tt lines 7-9 and 35-37 have no `if (Options.Generator.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage)` guard, unlike ResolverTemplate.tt and FormatterTemplate.tt. Compare with the README line 'To opt out, set [GeneratedMessagePackResolver(ExcludeFromCodeCoverage = false)]'.

hunches.claim: CompositeResolverTemplate emits the attribute without checking `Options.Generator.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage`, while every other template checks it. The new opt-out therefore has no effect on composite resolvers and their FormatterCache<T>. Users who set ExcludeFromCodeCoverage = false still get excluded generated code in the same assembly.

receipt_plan.detail: Compare CompositeResolverTemplate.tt:7-9 and :35-37, which emit the attribute unconditionally, with ResolverTemplate.tt:14-18, which wraps it in `if (Options.Generator.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage)`.

hunches.claim: The new public property GeneratedMessagePackResolverAttribute.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage is added to the public API, and the default of true means existing users get changed generated output without opting in. The analyzer reads the property by name via GetSingleNamedArgumentValue. An older MessagePack runtime paired with a newer generator is compatible, but a newer runtime with an older analyzer silently ignores the property.

receipt_plan.detail: Read AnalyzerUtilities.cs:76. The `is not false` default applies when the named argument is absent. Confirm the named argument is read from the attribute data and that the attribute is a source-defined type.

hunches.claim: The requirement says no new setting is needed and an opt-out is optional, but the change adds a new public API property GeneratedMessagePackResolverAttribute.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage and a new README-documented opt-out. This is permitted but expands the public API surface across four target frameworks. Whether the team wants that is not recorded.

receipt_plan.detail: Read GeneratedMessagePackResolverAttribute.cs:30-34 and the four PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt additions. The REQ-2297 acceptance criteria call an opt-out optional and give no maintainer decision.

hunches.claim: The attribute is guarded with #if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK. ExcludeFromCodeCoverage exists on netstandard2.0 as of .NET Core 2.0 only in newer targets. The requirement says generated code must be decorated, but netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework consumers, who may be a large share of the user base, get no exclusion. The README does document the gap.

receipt_plan.detail: Read the guard in all templates and README.md:1640. It contradicts the acceptance criterion that all generated code is decorated, unless 'attribute must exist there or be conditionally emitted' is accepted.

narrative: This run reviews reading B of REQ-2297 on branch review/ju26-issue-2297/B: Add the attribute to all generated types by default, plus provide an opt-out setting (e.g. MSBuild property or MessagePackKnownFormatter/GeneratorOptions flag) to disable it. Code: Adds a new public configuration option, reads it in the generator, and conditionally emits the attribute in templates; the other reading adds no option. As built on the branch: Emit [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on generated formatters and resolvers by default, with an opt-out via [GeneratedMessagePackResolver(ExcludeFromCodeCoverage = false)]
